title: Women scholars, then and now
hookLine: from Aisha to modern teachers of hadith and law

lines: GIVE US A DAY OF OUR OWN.
HE SETS A DAY AND TEACHES THEM.
cards: A group of women come to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, with a complaint. The men, they say, have taken all your time. Give us a day of our own.
And he does. He sets a day, goes to them, and teaches them. That small scene sits in the Book of Knowledge in Sahih al-Bukhari.
It's easy to miss. But it opens a long door: women asking for knowledge, getting it, and handing it on. Today: women scholars.

teach.b: Start with Aisha, the Prophet's wife. Hadith after hadith comes through her: how he prayed, how he lived at home, what he said in private.

Companions brought her their questions, and when she thought someone had reported the Prophet wrongly, she said so. Later scholars collected her corrections into a book of their own. Then follow the line forward.
Women learned hadith from their fathers and teachers, memorized long chains of narrators, and taught men as well as women.
One name worth knowing is Karima al-Marwaziyya, remembered for teaching Bukhari's great collection to students in Mecca; scholars traveled to hear it from her.
In our own time, the scholar Mohammad Akram Nadwi set out to gather the names and lives of women hadith scholars, in a study called al-Muhaddithat, the women who narrate hadith.

teach.h: WOMEN AND MEN, SIDE BY SIDE.
teach.b: The Qur'an speaks to women and men side by side, line after line: "Lo! men who surrender unto Allah, and women who surrender, and men who believe and women who believe."
Today women teach hadith, law and Qur'an in mosques, seminaries and universities across the Muslim world and beyond.
Schools and communities still differ on some questions about women's roles in leading prayer or giving rulings, and those debates are real.
But on the simple question of whether women taught the faith, the record answers plainly: from Aisha's room onward, they did.

how: Muslim women study and teach Qur'an, hadith and law in mosques, seminaries and universities, and communities often have women teachers who lead study circles for women and sometimes for mixed classes.

women who learned the faith deeply and taught it on

games.q: you're one of the women who tell the Prophet the men have taken all his time. what do you ask for?
o: a day of your own to learn.
to sit at the back of the men's class.
games.why: they asked for a day of their own, and he set one and taught them.

practice: Say the first name quietly, Aisha, and breathe; then the second, Karima, and breathe.

Then think of a woman who taught you something that matters, about faith, about life, about getting through, a grandmother, a teacher, an aunt, a neighbor, and say her name too. If you pray, ask God's mercy for each of them.

wordCard.voice: Women scholars. From Aisha and Karima to teachers today, women who learned the faith deeply and handed it on. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a woman of learning, a woman scholar.

carryVoice: Your line: they always taught. Every name you learn joins a very long list. Until tomorrow, then.
